paper_title: Recurrent Domain Incremental Adaptation of Time-Series Foundation Models

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Pretrained Time-Series Foundation Models (TSFMs) provide strong representations for downstream classification tasks. Yet adapting a TSFM under changing operating conditions remains challenging. A model must improve on each newly observed condition without sacrificing conditions it has already learned, often from only a small labeled calibration set and without knowing the operating condition at inference time. We find that this difficulty has an important geometric structure. Under an operating-condition shift, the embedding space of a TSFM does not move uniformly: some local regions change substantially, while others remain nearly unchanged. Consequently, a global adaptation can unnecessarily move embeddings that were already correctly classified. To address this, we propose the novel PACT (Piecewise Adaptation via Chart Transport). PACT partitions the frozen source embedding space into local charts and learns lightweight residual transports for the regions affected by each new condition. An explicit identity path is always retained, and a learned gate softly selects among the identity and accumulated transports for each input. The pretrained TSFM encoder, classifier head, and previously learned transports remain fixed. With only 5% labeled calibration data per arriving condition and no condition identity at test time, PACT maintains an average macro-F1 above 0.95 across a four-condition bearing-fault stream. Under homogeneous tasks and label spaces, similar retention-adaptation behavior is observed across public benchmarks. Code is available at https://github.com/Sachithx/PACT.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: Figure 1: Recurring operating conditions in machine fault diagnosis. New conditions (A, B) arrive with few labels, while earlier ones, including the source at = 3, continue to recur at inference without condition identity. Average macro-F1 over seen conditions degrades in the absence of Recurrent Domain Incremental Adaptation. 1 Preprint. Under Review. Pretrained time-series foundation models (TSFMs) have emerged as general-purpose representation learners for temporal data (Goswami et al., 2024; Woo et al., 2024; Ansari et al., 2024; Gong et al., 2026; Shi et al., 2025). An effective, efficient way to leverage these models for downstream classification tasks is to freeze the pretrained TSFM encoder and train only lightweight, taskspecific head. This avoids retraining large model and preserves the representation learned during pretraining. However, once initiated and deployed, the operating conditions may continue to change recurrently (Figure 1). Assuming homogeneous task and label space, consider fault-diagnosis system trained under specific machine load or rotational speed (Source). During its service life, it may encounter new operating conditions. Similarly, when human subjects are closely matched in age and behavior, similar changes can arise across users in wearable sensing, subjects in physiological monitoring, or sensor configurations in mobile systems. These conditions often arise recurrently, with only small amount of labeled data available for calibration. At inference time, the model may receive input samples from any condition encountered without being told which condition produced it. The model must therefore adapt to new conditions while still recognizing the old ones, given their recurrence. This adaptation is challenging even when the pretrained TSFM representation is strong. Figure 2 shows representative bearing-fault stream. The classifier with MOMENT-Large TSFM backbone (Goswami et al., 2024) performs well under its source condition, but its average Macro-F1 across all conditions drops sharply as conditions shift. Fine-tuning can recover performance on the new condition by updating model weights, but the same update changes parameters shared across all conditions and may degrade performance on earlier conditions. Regularization-based continual-learning methods reduce such changes, but this introduces the stability-plasticity trade-off: weak constraints allow adaptation but also lead to forgetting, whereas strong constraints preserve previous behavior at the expense of adaptation (Kirkpatrick et al., 2017; Aljundi et al., 2018; Zenke et al., 2017; Li & Hoiem, 2018). Methods that allocate condition-specific parameters reduce direct interference, but commonly rely on hard routing, task cues, or reliable estimates of the condition identity (Wang et al., 2022b). Furthermore, leveraging recent advances in strong TSFMs to address this core problem remains underexplored (Liang et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2026). Figure 2: MOMENT-large on the faultdiagnosis benchmark. Existing approaches differ in how they control adaptation, but they leave more fundamental question largely unanswered: Can classifier built on pretrained TSFM adapt to each new operating condition while retaining performance on the ones it already handles well? We study this question directly in the embedding space of frozen TSFMs. Our measurements reveal simple but important phenomenon: domain condition shift is highly non-uniform across the representation space. Some local regions degrade substantially after change in condition, whereas others remain nearly unaffected. Thus, the problem is not only how much to adapt, but also where adaptation is actually needed. Suppose an embedding already lies in region that remains correctly represented under new condition. For such an input, the desired correction may simply be the identity: nothing needs to change. An embedding in strongly shifted region, in contrast, may require non-zero correction before it is passed to the frozen classifier. single domain-wide transformation changes both. But if distribution shift acts locally, this motivates testing whether chart-specific corrections improve on single gated global transport. To this end, we introduce PACT (Piecewise Adaptation via Chart Transport), novel Domain Incremental Learning (DIL) method that leverages pretrained TSFM. PACT partitions the source embedding space into local regions, which we call charts. When new domain condition arrives, it learns lightweight residual transport within each supported chart using the available labeled calibration examples. The adaptation then changes the embedding presented to the classifier head, not Preprint. Under Review. the representation model or its decision boundary. Once condition is learned, its transports are frozen; later conditions add new transports without modifying the TSFM backbone, classifier head, or previously learned corrections. At inference time, the condition identity is unavailable, and an input may come from any condition. PACT therefore learns chart-specific gate that softly combines the available condition transports. Importantly, this mixture always includes the unmodified source embedding as an explicit identity path. The gate can therefore apply large correction when the evidence favors an adapted branch, combine several plausible corrections when conditions overlap, or remain close to the original representation when adaptation is unnecessary. The identity path also makes the remaining source of degradation explicit. Because the TSFM encoder, classifier head, and previously learned transports never change, newly arriving condition cannot overwrite these components. An earlier prediction can change only if routing moves its embedding through non-identity transport. When the gate assigns all mass to the identity path, PACT exactly reproduces the frozen models prediction. More generally, we derive margin-based condition showing when non-identity-routed correction is still small enough to preserve the predicted class. This is conditional preservation result rather than zero-forgetting guarantee: the remaining error comes from routing and the magnitude of the applied correction. We evaluate PACT under recurrent condition shifts on five time-series domain adaptation benchmarks: bearing-fault diagnosis (FD), HHAR, Sleep-EDF, WISDM, and UCI-HAR. Under homogeneous labels and task spaces, with observed relative shifts from the source condition, the streams cover changes in operating condition, users, and subjects, and we never provide domain identity at inference time. We compare against frozen, fine-tuning, regularization, distillation, test-time adaptation, source-free adaptation, and domain-incremental baselines, all with matched calibration budgets. On the frozen Sundial backbone, PACT consistently outperforms the average macro-F1 on FD, WISDM, HHAR, and UCIHAR, while keeping forgetting below 0.05. The same mechanism transfers across eight classification-pretrained TSFMs, forecasting-pretrained TSFMs, and task-specific encoders, indicating that PACT is independent of the backbone architecture. Ablations further show that the two parts of the method are complementary: local transports provide adaptation, while learned identity-preserving routing is needed to avoid applying those corrections indiscriminately. The contributions of this work are summarized as follows: We show that condition shifts cause heterogeneous degradation across frozen embedding regions, motivating local correction. We propose first-of-its-kind PACT that combines chart-specific residual transports with identity-aware routing for label-efficient domain-incremental adaptation, while keeping the encoder and head frozen. We evaluate PACT on five benchmarks and eight backbones, demonstrating effective adaptation and retention, and we include ablations that examine its key components.

sections.title: 2 RELATED WORK
sections.content: Time-series foundation models provide transferable representations for downstream tasks with limited supervision (Liang et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2026). Adapting these representations to changing conditions remains an active area of research. MAPU and its evidential extension, E-MAPU, adapt time-series feature extractors through temporal imputation and uncertainty-aware alignment (Ragab et al., 2023; 2026). Alternatively, TATO adapts input transformations while keeping forecasting TSFM frozen (Qiu et al., 2026). These approaches address target-domain adaptation; our focus is sequential classification with fixed label set, where samples from earlier conditions remain relevant after each update. PACT therefore preserves both the pretrained encoder and source-trained head while learning corrections from small labeled calibration sets. Regularization methods such as EWC, MAS, and SI constrain changes to important parameters, while Learning without Forgetting preserves previous outputs through distillation (Kirkpatrick et al., 2017; Aljundi et al., 2018; Zenke et al., 2017; Li & Hoiem, 2018). Test-time methods adapt using unlabeled observations: TENT minimizes prediction entropy, CoTTA addresses continually changing distributions, and EATA explicitly regularizes adaptation to reduce forgetting (Wang et al., 2021; 2022a; Niu et al., 2022). For time-series classification, DualCD addresses domain-incremental learning through causal feature disentanglement and intervention (Liu et al., 2026b). These methods 3 Preprint. Under Review. motivate the same adaptation-retention challenge, but differ from our adaptation constraints. PACT freezes previously learned corrections and updates their routing, preserving their parameters without guaranteeing unchanged predictions. S-Prompts learns independent domain prompts and uses nearest-neighbor domain identification at inference (Wang et al., 2022b). RanPAC combines random projections with accumulated class statistics for classand domain-incremental learning, while EASE expands representation subspaces for class-incremental learning (McDonnell et al., 2023; Zhou et al., 2024). SEMA further learns mixtures of adapters with adaptive module expansion (Wang et al., 2025). PASS generates training features around stored class prototypes to preserve earlier classes during classifier updates (Zhu et al., 2021). FeCAM uses class-specific means and covariances to classify an observation by its distance to each class distribution (Goswami et al., 2023). PACT assigns each embedding to source-defined chart, where learned gate blends the identity path with condition-specific corrections before the frozen head predicts the class (see Appendix C.4 for the comparison with PASS and FeCAM).

sections.content: 3.1 PROBLEM FORMULATION We consider recurrent domain-incremental time-series classification over sequence of domain conditions D0, . . . , DT sharing fixed label set. pretrained encoder fθ produces an aggregated, source-standardized embedding Rp for each series, and linear head hϕ is trained on the fully labeled source domain D0; both remain frozen during subsequent adaptation. Each new domain condition Dd provides few-labeled calibration set comprising fraction ρ of its training split. Source and calibration embeddings are retained, while the raw series signal and class labels of the source or any previous domain condition are not stored or revisited. After observing the condition through step t, the objective is to classify samples from any domain condition without access to their identity, using an embedding-space correction Ψt: ˆy = arg maxy[hϕ(Ψt(z))]y. We assume competent source representation and domain shifts that preserve the underlying labeling function and admit small residual corrections within adequately covered regions of the source embedding space. Furthermore, the concept shift is outside our scope. 3.2 PACT: PIECEWISE ADAPTATION VIA CHART TRANSPORT PACT (Piecewise Adaptation via Chart Transport) adapts frozen host through local residual corrections in embedding space. The observations in Figure 3 motivate this design: degradation varies across source-defined regions, local corrections reduce held-out error, and target-fitted global correction can degrade source performance. Accordingly, PACT partitions the source embedding space into fixed charts, learns chart-specific transports for each arriving condition, and routes inputs through the accumulated transports without requiring condition identity. sections.title: 4 RESULTS
sections.content: 4.1 EXPERIMENTAL SETUP Datasets. We evaluate on five time-series classification benchmarks spanning distinct condition shift types: FD (Paderborn bearing-fault diagnosis; 4 operating conditions, 3 classes), WISDM (36 users, 6 activities), HHAR (9 users, 6 activities), UCI-HAR (30 subjects, 6 activities), and SleepEDF (20 subjects, 5 sleep stages) (Lessmeier et al., 2016; Kwapisz et al., 2011; Stisen et al., 2015; Anguita et al., 2013; Kemp et al., 2000). Evaluation protocol. Each stream begins with labeled source condition and introduces one target condition at time. After each update, we evaluate all conditions seen so far on held-out examples without providing condition identity at inference. FD uses all four operating conditions, and HHAR uses all nine users. WISDM, UCI-HAR, and Sleep-EDF use nine subjects per stream, with subject composition and order varying across streams. Table 1 reports the mean over three training seeds and four fixed streams per dataset. All methods use the same streams and data splits. Methods that use target class labels receive the same class-stratified calibration examples: 5% of the arriving 6 Preprint. Under Review. conditions training split on FD, HHAR, and Sleep-EDF, up to 450 examples on WISDM, and up to 100 on UCI-HAR. Appendix B.1 lists the exact streams. Backbones and PACT configuration. The main comparison uses frozen Sundial (Liu et al., 2025). We test backbone transfer with classification-pretrained Mantis and UniShape (Feofanov et al., 2026a;b; Liu et al., 2026a), forecasting-pretrained MOMENT, Chronos-Bolt, and Moirai (Goswami et al., 2024; Ansari et al., 2024; Woo et al., 2024), and task-specific TSLANet and PatchTST (Eldele et al., 2024; Nie et al., 2023). Each backbone is frozen during domain incremental adaptation. Condition identity is unavailable at inference. Unless stated otherwise, PACT uses rank-8 transports, gate temperature τ = 0.5, and the chart count chosen based on validation-split performance. Transports and gates are each trained for 200 epochs with the AdamW optimizer at learning rate of 103; further implementation details are provided in the supplement (Appendix B). Baselines. All baselines operate on the same frozen Sundial embeddings and receive the same domain-condition orders, splits, and calibration-label budget. We compare against non-adaptive frozen source model and nearest-class-mean (NCM) prototypes; test-time and source-free adaptation with CoTTA, EATA, MAPU, ACCUP, and TENT (Wang et al., 2022a; Niu et al., 2022; Ragab et al., 2023; Gong et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2021); head fine-tuning and the regularization or distillation methods EWC, MAS, LwF, and source-distillation, which combines target cross-entropy with KL divergence from the frozen source head (Kirkpatrick et al., 2017; Aljundi et al., 2018; Li & Hoiem, 2018); and the domain-incremental methods S-Prompts and DualCD (Wang et al., 2022b; Liu et al., 2026b). MAPU, ACCUP, and TENT are label-free; CoTTA, EATA, and the domain-incremental methods are adapted to this embedding/head setting, with details in the supplement. We also compare PACT with two rehearsal baselines. Embedding replay stores embeddings and their class labels. DER++ (Buzzega et al., 2020) stores raw windows, class labels, and logits in reservoir whose capacity is set using the byte size of PACTs retained embedding array. Metrics. Let At,j denote macro-F1 on the held-out test split of domain after adaptation through domain t. After the full stream, we report average macro-F1 AMF1 = 1 j=0 AT,j (), together +1 with two lower-is-better forgetting measures, relative forgetting RF = 1 j=0 [pj AT,j]+/(pj + ϵ) and performance relative forgetting PRF = 1 j=0 (1AT,j)[pj AT,j]+/(pj +ϵ), where pj = maxjl<T Al,j is the peak score on domain j, [u]+ = max(0, u), and ϵ = 109. RF normalizes each peak-to-final drop by that peak, while PRF additionally weights the drop by how poor the final score is, following DualCD (Liu et al., 2026b). Its largest gains were on FD and WISDM, where it exceeded the strongest baseline shown by 11.15 and 8.34 percentage points, respectively. The margin was smaller on HHAR (0.71 points), and LwF led PACT by 0.09 points on Sleep-EDF. PACTs relative forgetting ranged from 0.0021 on FD to 0.0425 on UCI-HAR. Figure 5 compares PACT with two rehearsal-based methods on the same four streams per dataset. PACT achieved higher final AMF1 than both replay methods on FD and WISDM, exceeding embedding replay by 4.79 and 1.45 percentage points, respectively. Embedding replay led PACT by 2.81 points on HHAR and 3.05 points on UCI-HAR, while DER++ led by 3.24 points on Sleep-EDF. PACT achieved these results while discarding past class labels after each transport bank was fitted. When both methods were limited to 512 historical embeddings, PACT retained 4.38-point AMF1 advantage over embedding replay on FD, while replay led on the other four datasets  (Table 5)  . Across four streams per dataset, PACT had smaller final decline in source macro-F1 than embedding replay and head fine-tuning on all five datasets. The decline ranged from 0.02 percentage points on FD to 6.16 points on UCI-HAR (Appendix C.5). In separate simulated FD revisit, held-out macro-F1 on condition remained at 0.9748 after learning and C, and macro-F1 on condition remained at 0.9137 after learning D. Both revisits used the learned gate without condition identity at inference. The benchmark streams evaluate recurrence by testing held-out examples from previously seen conditions after each update. Transfer across backbones. Because PACT requires only an embedding and frozen head, it applies unchanged to task-specific encoders and to forecasting-pretrained TSFMs used purely as feature extractors. Figure 6 reports this across eight hosts. Mantis is strongest on FD, WISDM, HHAR, and UCI-HAR, reaching AMF1 of 0.985, 0.967, 0.925, and 0.922, while TSLANet is also strong on Sleep-EDF at 0.708. The spread within the dataset is nevertheless substantial: UCI-HAR ranges from 0.517 (PatchTST) to 0.922 (Mantis). PACT is therefore architecturally portable, but the separability of the frozen representation bounds what any embedding-space correction can recover. The columns cover cell classification-pretrained, forecasting-pretrained, and task-specific encoders. 4.3 ABLATION STUDY Impact of residual transports and routing. Figure 7 separates plasticity from retention. Head fine-tuning increases AMF1 relative to the frozen model but incurs the highest PRF across all datasets, adapting at the cost of retention. Ungated transports raise AMF1 further, yet still forget Preprint. Under Review. Figure 7: Component ablation on frozen Sundial. Removing transports gives the non-adaptive source model; head fine-tuning updates only the classifier; removing the gate uses an ungated transport mixture. Full PACT combines rank-8 chart transports with learned soft routing. by correcting indiscriminately. Adding the learned gate gives both the best AMF1 and the lowest PRF among adaptive variants on all five datasets, so local correction and identity-preserving routing are complementary rather than alternatives. The effect is largest on FD and WISDM and smallest for Sleep-EDF, consistent with their more overlapping embedding distributions. Effect of chart count and placement. With rank-8 transports, the identity branch, and learned routing retained throughout, increasing the chart count from = 1 to = 4 improved AMF1 on FD and all three activity datasets  (Table 2)  . FD improved further at = 8, while the three activity datasets achieved their highest AMF1 at = 4. At fixed transport and gate capacity, source k-means outperformed random-projection partitions on all four streams for each of the five tested datasetK configurations, including second UCI-HAR comparison at = 8 (Appendix C.3). sections.title: 5 CONCLUSION
sections.content: We introduced PACT, frozen-host method for recurrent domain incremental adaptation of TSFMs. Across five benchmarks, the frozen-Sundial comparison yields strong AMF1 for PACT while keeping forgetting below 0.05. The eight-backbone study shows that the mechanism transfers across architectures and highlights the importance of representation quality: Mantis leads on all datasets. Component, rank, and routing ablations support the three design choices of local transport, low rank, and soft identity-preserving routing. 10 Preprint. Under Review.

sections.title: 6 LIMITATIONS AND FUTURE WORK
sections.content: PACT relies on the quality of the frozen representation and the coverage of its source-defined charts. If the encoder fails to distinguish classes under new condition, embedding corrections have limited information with which to recover them. Target examples far from source support may also share chart despite requiring different corrections. Adaptive chart refinement and soft chart assignment could improve coverage and reduce sensitivity near chart boundaries. Retention also depends on routing. Overlapping conditions remain difficult to distinguish, as reflected in the oracle-routing gaps on HHAR and UCI-HAR. Although the identity branch preserves access to the original classifier, gate refitting can change earlier predictions. Improved routing and calibration could help preserve source predictions while maintaining adaptation to new conditions. PACT retains source and calibration embeddings with condition assignments, and its transport bank grows as conditions arrive. The bounded-memory experiments show that reducing the retained history can affect performance, particularly on the activity datasets. More effective embedding selection and transport consolidation are therefore useful directions. Finally, calibration imbalance and missing classes can reduce adaptation quality. Future work could investigate label-efficient calibration strategies and evaluation on naturally recurring streams with longer deployment horizons.

Eight of the 24 target chartcondition cells were masked. Proposition 1 certified 889 of the 891 initially correct source predictions. Among 1,661 initially correct target predictions, 10 became incorrect (0.60%). The median identity weight was approximately zero both for target predictions that remained correct and for those that became incorrect. On this stream, the gate distinguished source from target examples, while its identity weight alone provided little indication of whether target prediction would be damaged. sections.title: D SUPPLEMENTARY FIGURES
sections.content: We provide additional visualizations of sequential adaptation, embedding corrections, and domain structure. Figures 10 and 13 show performance along individual domain orders, complementing the aggregate results in the main text. Figures 11 and 12 illustrate PACTs corrections and the variation in domain overlap within frozen representations. Figure 10: Performance throughout domain-incremental streams. PACT and comparison methods are evaluated with MOMENT-Large, Sundial, and TSLANet along the domain orders shown on the horizontal axes. Each point reports performance over the domains observed so far, using the metric indicated on the vertical axis. Calibration budgets are specified below each panel, and endpoint annotations report final scores for the displayed runs. 20 Preprint. Under Review. Figure 11: Embedding corrections on HHAR. Left: source embeddings from User-1. Middle: uncorrected embeddings from User-7 and User-0. Right: embeddings after PACT transport, with arrows indicating projected displacements. Colors denote activity classes; triangles and squares identify the two arriving domains. Faded circles provide the source reference in the middle and right panels. Figure 12: Domain structure in frozen representations. For each dataset, t-SNE projections of frozen TSLANet embeddings are colored by domain, alongside pairwise Euclidean distances between domain centroids in the original embedding space. The projections illustrate varying degrees of domain overlap; centroid distances summarize differences in domain means. 21 Preprint. Under Review. Figure 13: Per-domain performance during sequential adaptation. Matrices show macro-F1 across eight backbones for the domain orders indicated above each dataset. Entry (t, j) reports performance on domain after learning through step t. Diagonal entries record performance when domain first appears; subsequent entries in each column track its retention. Blank entries correspond to domains not yet observed.
